Noisome

/NOY-suhm/ - the stress falls on NOY · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Noisome means highly offensive, especially in smell.

By late afternoon the fish stalls' runoff gathered along the gutter, and shoppers crossed the lane to keep clear of the noisome trickle.

Worked Example

The castle's moat was its plainest defense and its foulest: two hundred years of the town's drains emptied into water that never moved. Chroniclers wrote that besieging soldiers who waded it came out retching, and that summer garrisons bribed one another to escape wall duty on the leeward side. No catapult was ever aimed at the moat, and none was needed.

Noisome is the exact word for that moat, because it means highly offensive, especially in smell — and the especially is doing real work. Noisome comes from annoy, not noise: a noisome thing harms or disgusts, and most noisome things happen to stink. It is the broadest of this unit's four foul words, wide enough to cover harmful fumes with no smell at all.

How Noisome Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

vile

vile: repellently bad in any way at all

sickening

sickening: turning the stomach

Antonyms

wholesome

wholesome: healthy and clean — built with the same -some ending

inviting

inviting: drawing you toward it

How Strong Is It? — unpleasant → offensive → noisome

unpleasant vs. noisome

unpleasant vs. noisome: Unpleasant is the mild rung — a smell you would rather be without, easy enough to wave away.

offensive vs. noisome

offensive vs. noisome: Offensive goes further than unpleasant — people complain and keep their distance — but noisome claims the most: foul enough, or harmful enough, to drive them out entirely.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of noisome.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — noi

Root — noi: harm, vexation (Middle English noy, clipped from annoy)

Suffix — -some

Suffix — -some: causing, tending to (as in troublesome)

Put it together

Put it together: Noi (harm) + -some (causing) = causing harm or vexation. The same builder's suffix gives troublesome and wearisome — and wholesome, its bright opposite. Noise never enters into it: a noisome cellar can be silent as stone.

Use the root in a new word: annoy

Use the root in a new word: annoy: Medieval English used annoy for real injury — a garrison could annoy the enemy with arrows — before the word softened into pinpricks.

Word Choice

literary / old-fashioned

Noisome is the broadest of this unit's four foul words: it means offensive — usually to the nose, but harmful fumes, a noisome pit, even a noisome policy all fit the bill. Fetid is standing air and water; putrid is active decay; rancid is spoiled fat. And despite its spelling, noisome says nothing about sound.
